What is Entire?

98:
99:
100:

Entire is the git forge for AI-native teams. The Entire CLI captures every AI coding agent session, so the reasoning behind the code stays with the git repo, right next to your code. Then, Continuous Memory (Entire Graph + Entire Brain) turns those sessions into living knowledge for your agents. Your repo learns from every attempt, every fix, every decision, and your agents get smarter because of it.

A debugger for agent mistakes

196: 04 197:

Connect your repository

198:
199:
    200:
  1. 201:

    Sign in

    202:

    Everyone on the team signs in to Entire with Sign in with GitHub and authorizes the Entire GitHub App when prompted. You can do this at any time, before or after the next step.

    203:
    2. 204:
  2. 205:

    GitHub organization admin: import the repository

    206:

    A GitHub organization admin installs the Entire GitHub App on the organization by following the onboarding. Nothing repository-related appears for anyone in the team until this step is done.

    207:

    Sign-in order doesn't matter, but the repository and its sessions only show up after the admin has configured access.

    208:

    Once the admin has imported the repository, it appears for the whole team. No invites and no permission setup: access follows the GitHub collaborator list, so everyone keeps the same roles they have on GitHub.

    209:
    Changes can take up to an hour to sync. If the repository is missing from your list, ask your organization admin.

Start your first checkpoint

    Install Entire, then enable it from your repository

    223:

    225: 
    # macOS; see Resources for other platforms
226: brew install --cask entireio/tap/entire
227: 
228: cd your-repo
229: entire enable --agent codex
    230:
    231: 232:

    Replace codex with your agent's integration name. Start a new agent session, ask it to make a focused change, and review the result.

    233:

239: git commit -m "Build my first feature with Entire"

259: 06 260:

Turn on Trails

Optional 261:
262:

You'll see Trails in action during our demo. To use it in your own repository:

263: 264:
    265:
  1. 266:

    Request access from an Entiron after you onboard on Entire

    267:

    Trails is behind a feature flag. Once you've signed up, fill in the Trails access form and someone from the Entire team will enable Trails for you.

    268:
    2. 269:
  2. 270:

    Enable Trails in your repository

    271:

    Open your repository in Entire, go to Settings → General, and turn on Runners, Auto build on push, and Trails. This requires admin permission on the repository.

    272:
    Each Trail is currently backed by a GitHub PR for CI.
    273:
    3. 274:
  3. 275:

    Add the default Runners

    276:

    Runners evaluate each Trail and publish findings. From the repository root, run:

    277:
    278:
    Shell
    279: 
    entire runner setup -y
    280:
    281: 282:

    Then commit and push the generated .entire/ files.

    283:
    4. 284:
  4. 285:

    You or your agent: create a Trail and work normally

    286:

    Your coding agent already knows how to use Trails through the CLI, so just ask it to create one. Or run:

    287:
    288:
    Shell
    289: 
    entire trail create
    290:
    291: 292:

    Commit and push to the Trail branch as usual. The Trail updates automatically, Runners evaluate each push, and your team can review and merge from the Trail.

    293:

299: 07 300:

Continuous Memory

301:
302:

Optional: only if you are building with Entire Graph/Brain.

303: 304:
305:

AInstall and activate entire-graph

306:

You or your agents can install the entire-graph plugin. Activate it once per repository:

307:
308:
Shell
309: 
entire plugin install graph
310: entire graph init-agents --repo .
311:
312: 313:

The second command creates .entire/graph-agent.md with the agent instructions, and adds a short block to your AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md telling your agents to use entire-graph.

314:

Commit those three files so it applies to your whole team, then start a fresh agent session. You'll know it worked when your agent's first move is entire-graph search instead of a grep.

315: 316:

Start using entire-graph

317:

Restart the agent so it picks up the new instructions, then ask in plain language: Where is request routing implemented? The agent runs graph queries, reads the code the graph points to, and answers with citations.

318:

To see what it saved you, run:

319:
320:
Shell
321: 
entire graph stats --repo .
322:
323: 324:

It reads your Claude Code session transcripts, counts how many times your agent used the graph instead of grepping and reading files, and estimates the tokens it saved. For how entire-graph works, installation, and troubleshooting, see the Graph docs .

325:
326: 327:
328:

BInstall entire-brain

329:

Make sure the Entire CLI and entire-graph are installed first (steps above).

330:
Without entire-graph, setup reports the semantic index as unavailable; sessions, docs and facts still work. Without the Entire CLI there are no sessions to read, and entire-brain falls back to code, docs and Git history.
331:
332:
Shell
333: 
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/entireio/entire-brain/main/scripts/get-brain.sh | bash
334:
335: 336:

The script downloads a prebuilt binary, checks it against the release checksums, and registers it with the CLI as the entire-brain plugin.

337: 338:
339: Or build from source 340:

Needs Go 1.27+, Git 2.36+, the Entire CLI on your PATH, and a C compiler for Graph's tree-sitter bindings.

341:
342:
Shell
343: 
git clone https://github.com/entireio/entire-brain.git
344: cd entire-brain
345: ./scripts/install.sh
346:
347: 348:

This builds and registers entire-brain and entire-graph. It does not initialize a repository's memory or install the watcher. Then cd to the project repository where you want Brain and run:

349:
350:
Shell
351: 
entire brain setup
352:
353: 354:
355: 356:

Activate your agent

357:

From your project repository, install the agent instructions:

358:
359:
Shell
360: 
entire brain init-agents
361:
362: 363:

This embeds your existing sessions (if any) and creates or updates the agent instructions at .entire/agent-guide.md. Rerunning the command replaces this file. It also updates AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md with references to the guide inside managed blocks; your text outside those blocks is preserved.

364:

Review the generated files and commit them together when the instructions should apply to your team. When entire-graph is installed, the guide tells agents to use entire-brain for prior decisions and entire-graph to locate and inspect code. Restart your agent or reload its repository instructions so it picks up the guide.

365: 366:

Using an MCP client?

367:

Print this repository's configuration:

368:
369:
Shell
370: 
entire brain mcp --print-config
371:
372: 373:

Then register it with an MCP-capable client. For example, in Claude Code:

374:
375:
Shell
376: 
claude mcp add entire-brain -- entire brain mcp
377:
378: 379:

See the agent integration guide and coordination contract for more setup details.

      sweep, the walls take their paint, furniture is lowered in piece by piece.
      A few trees and shrub clusters grow slowly across the build while grass
      creeps out from the house and the drive is laid.
    - 3D: colours are authored in sRGB but glTF factors are linear, so every
      finish rendered washed out; convert them. Collinear duplicate walls are
      merged before building, which removes the flicker between two leaves.
    - The palette card is minimised to a name, a colour strip and arrows.

    feat(air): solve the breeze through the whole floor and set it moving
    
    A potential-flow solve over each floor and the ground around it: walls are
    solid, windows and open doors are resistive cuts sized by their height, the
    wind is a free stream from any compass point. Air changes, mean indoor speed
    and still-air share come from the solved flux per room. A new Air view draws
    it live: speed as light, particles advected by the field, inlets and outlets
    marked by the sign of the flow, a wind rose and a best-wind ranking.

FAQs
When and where is neatHack?
neatHack is a 48-hour online hackathon on October 10–12, 2026, starting Saturday at 12:30 PM IST. The kickoff call is at 9:00 AM IST on October 10. Submissions open October 12 at 7:00 PM IST, with a planned close around 11:55 PM IST. The final cutoff will be announced on Discord. Winners are announced on October 16.
Can I build with a team?
Come solo or in a team of 1–4 people. Every member must register on Luma using the same team name, and each person can join only one team.
What can I build beforehand?
You can plan your idea in advance, but all code must be written between the start on October 10 and the deadline on October 12. Finished or half-built projects cannot be brought into the event. Use neatlogs throughout development to capture traces, investigate failures, identify bottlenecks and improve your agent.
How many tracks are there?
There is one track, Build an agent that works (literally), and every project competes for the same prizes. You can build a single agent or a system of several agents. The example tasks are ideas, not separate tracks.
Do I have to use a partner technology?
Yes. Every project must use neatlogs, Entire and cfo.ai, with a clear role for each in building the agent or planning its business. Your demo must cover all three tools.
What do I need to submit?
Each team submits one project as a public quote post of the official neatlogs submission post on X before the confirmed cutoff. Use Submit on X to open the draft, fill in your team, name, project, public repository and demo link, keep the official post attached, then publish on X. Include supporting evidence in your repository. Include a demo video of three minutes or less and a public code repository. The video must explicitly cover neatlogs, Entire and cfo.ai: architecture, implementation, runtime, reasoning and result for each tool. Judges must be able to verify that commits were made during the hackathon. Submissions open October 12 at 7:00 PM IST, with a planned close around 11:55 PM IST. Submit any time during this window; the final cutoff will be announced on Discord. Entries after the confirmed cutoff will not be judged. The Submit on X button appears once the window and official post are live. Opening the draft alone does not submit your project. neatlogs and cfo.ai will engage with the first 50 quote tweets.
How are projects judged?
Mentors score each project using the published criteria. The agent is worth 30% of the final score, the use of neatlogs, Entire and cfo.ai is worth 25%, and the demo video is worth 20%. Building in public is worth 15%, and usefulness and originality are worth 10%. The judges' decision is final, and the community winner is judged separately.
How does the community winner work?
The community winner goes to the project that generates the strongest genuine community interest during the hackathon. We look at the quality and creativity of the product and demo, the quality of the launch and content, shares and discussion, genuine engagement, and whether people are excited enough to try, share or talk about it. Existing audience size or follower count does not decide the winner. The project must use neatlogs, Entire and cfo.ai, but partner usage is not part of community winner scoring. Bought likes or bot activity will disqualify a team.
What are the conduct rules?
Be respectful in Discord and all event spaces. Harassment, spam or plagiarism will result in removal from the hackathon.
Does the AWS allowance cover AI model APIs?
No. Bedrock isn’t included in the hackathon AWS accounts. The $25 allowance per team or solo covers only the approved AWS services. For models, verify the team leader’s check-in email at neatlogs.com/hackathon/models to claim a separate shared LiteLLM key with a $20 budget for Nova and Claude. Your AWS access email includes the permitted services and usage rules.
Where can I get help and credits?
Join neatlogs.com/discord for official neatHack communication. AWS credits go to the first 350 teams to complete web check-in. Fully checked-in teams and solo participants can claim one shared $20 LiteLLM key at neatlogs.com/hackathon/models, while keys are available. Crustdata gives 5,000 credits to everyone participating. Dodo Payments credits are for the top three winners only: $5,000 for first, $3,000 for second and $1,000 for third. Each winner gets 3 months of neatlogs Pro (worth $1500). Access and redemption details will be published with the resources. Workshops and office hours run on both days.

1: # Architect Intelligence Platform (AIP)
2: 
3: **An explainable multi-agent AI framework for architectural design, interior
4: planning, Vastu analysis, cost prediction and client-centric design automation.**
5: 
6: Give it a plot and a brief. It returns a buildable scheme — floorplans,
7: elevations, sections, a furnished interior, an explainable Vastu report, a
8: costed bill of quantities and a 3D walkthrough — reviewed by a committee of
9: thirteen independent critics, with every verdict traceable to its evidence.
10: 
11: It runs on a laptop. It needs no GPU, no Docker and no cloud account. Model
12: spend is **$0.00**, and the test suite asserts that as an invariant.
13: 
14: ```bash
15: cd backend
16: python -m venv .venv && .venv/Scripts/pip install -e ".[dev]"   # Windows
17: .venv/Scripts/python -m uvicorn aip.api.app:app --port 8000
18: ```
19: 
20: Then open **http://127.0.0.1:8000** for the architect studio, or
21: **http://127.0.0.1:8000/embed/demo** to see the client-facing widget embedded in
22: a (fictional) practice's website.
23: 
24: ---
25: 
26: ## Why this is not another AI design tool
27: 
28: A single model asked to "design a house" optimises one opaque internal
29: objective. Architecture is irreducibly multi-objective: daylight fights privacy,
30: Vastu fights structural economy, generous rooms fight the budget. AIP makes that
31: conflict explicit and resolvable.
32: 
33: **Thirteen critics review every candidate scheme. Ten of them are analytical.**
34: 
35: | | Critic | What it actually does |
36: |---|---|---|
37: | ▪ | Building Code Officer | NBC of India 2016 + local DCR, clause by clause. Breaches disqualify outright. |
38: | ▪ | Daylight Analyst | BRE average daylight factor per room, corrected by real solar geometry for the site's latitude |
39: | ▪ | Ventilation Analyst | Openable-area ratios, true cross-ventilation detection, air changes per hour against prevailing wind |
40: | ▪ | Privacy Analyst | Ray-cast sightlines from the entrance, topological depth to bedrooms, WC-onto-living detection |
41: | ▪ | Circulation Analyst | Reachability, walking distance between functionally-related rooms, circulation overhead |
42: | ▪ | Accessibility Analyst | Door clear widths, wheelchair turning circles, step-free entry (Harmonised Guidelines 2021) |
43: | ▪ | Spatial Quality Analyst | Proportion, compactness, largest inscribed square — catches rooms that meet their area and still cannot be furnished |
44: | ▪ | Structural Reviewer | Span economy, grid regularity, inter-floor load-path continuity |
45: | ▪ | Vastu Reasoner | 29 formally encoded rules with citations, reconciled against modern building science |
46: | ▪ | Quantity Surveyor | Takeoff from geometry, priced against a regional schedule, Monte Carlo risk band |
47: | ○ | Design Coherence Reviewer | *generative* — does it read as one deliberate piece of architecture? |
48: | ○ | Brief Fidelity Reviewer | *generative* — did it deliver what the client actually asked for? |
49: | ○ | Livability Reviewer | *generative* — how will this be to live in, day to day, for years? |
50: 
51: The analytical ten cost nothing, run in microseconds, and are exactly
52: reproducible. They are what stops a language model talking a bad design past the
53: committee: **the daylight critic is not persuadable, it is arithmetic.**
54: 
55: ## Does the committee actually help?
56: 
57: Run the ablation yourself:
58: 
59: ```bash
60: cd backend && .venv/Scripts/python -m aip.evaluation.harness
61: ```
62: 
63: Eight benchmark briefs, three selection procedures, same candidate pool, same
64: seed — so the difference isolates the *procedure*, not the generator's luck.
65: 
66: | Arm | Composite quality | Compliance | Vastu | **Critical code breaches** |
67: |---|---|---|---|---|
68: | Single weighted objective | 0.8397 | 0.8080 | 0.7355 | **11** |
69: | Committee, no Pareto step | 0.8456 | 0.8421 | 0.7401 | **7** |
70: | **Full MACC consensus** | **0.8520** | **0.8750** | 0.7220 | **6** |
71: 
72: The headline is the last column: **the committee produces 45% fewer critical
73: statutory breaches than a single weighted objective.** Compliance rises 8.3%.
74: 
75: Note that Vastu goes *down* 1.8% in the full arm. That is the mechanism working
76: as designed, not a defect: the consensus trades a little Vastu compliance for a
77: large gain in code compliance, because a statutory breach is a hard constraint
78: and a Vastu preference is not. Reporting it is the point — a system that only
79: showed you its wins would not be one you could trust with the trade-offs.
80: 
81: Explainability scores 1.00 across all arms because every arm uses the same
82: finding generator; it measures the platform, not the difference between arms.
83: 
84: ## The agents negotiate, they do not just vote
85: 
86: Selecting the best of three schemes cannot fix a flaw all three share. So after
87: the committee votes, a **manager–worker consensus protocol** takes the winner and
88: negotiates it against seven constraints — three hard, four soft — each owned by
89: the agent responsible for repairing it.
90:

103: 
104: A proposal is accepted **only when re-measuring the whole design shows a net
105: gain**, and hard constraints are weighted three times a soft one. Those two rules
106: together mean the design can never end a round worse than it began, and no
107: accumulation of comfort gains can outrank fixing a statutory breach. Both are
108: asserted by tests.
109: 
110: When a brief genuinely cannot be built, the loop says so — and the agent that
111: owns the failing constraint has to explain why it cannot help:
112: 
113: ```
114:    [no change] cost_estimator: already specified at the lowest finish tier, so no
115:    further step-down exists. The overrun is driven by the size of the programme,
116:    not by the specification, and cannot be closed without the client either
117:    raising the budget or dropping accommodation.
118: outcome         converged   hard open 0
119:    STILL OPEN [soft] cost.within_budget: 310% of budget
120: ```
121: 
122: An agent that owns a failing constraint and stays silent is indistinguishable
123: from an agent that never ran.
124: 
125: ## The Vastu engine
126: 
127: Most Vastu software is a lookup table that returns a verdict with no reasoning
128: and no way to disagree. This is a defeasible rule system over a formally encoded
129: corpus. Every rule carries five things a lookup table does not:
130: 
131: 1. **Provenance** — Manasara, Mayamata, Vishvakarma Prakasha, Samarangana
132:    Sutradhara, Brihat Samhita, or an honest `contemporary` label where no text
133:    exists. The treatises disagree with each other; naming the source lets you
134:    weigh a rule instead of obeying it.
135: 2. **Traditional rationale** — what the text says the rule is *for*.
136: 3. **Modern rationale** — the climatic or functional mechanism that does or does
137:    not support it.
138: 4. **Modern validity** ∈ [0,1] — how much survives that scrutiny.
139: 5. **Remedy** — the concrete change that resolves a violation.
140: 
141: A rule's effective weight is `w × (t + (1−t) × modern_validity)`, where `t` is
142: the client's stance. At `t=1` the classical corpus governs completely. At `t=0`
143: only rules with a demonstrable physical basis retain influence — and the report
144: tells you exactly which rules lost weight and why.
145: 
146: That is the traditional/modern reconciliation, and it is arithmetic you can
147: audit rather than a claim.

160: 
161: ### The knowledge graph — reasoning past the corpus
162: 
163: An authored corpus can only judge a placement some text troubled to write down.
164: Every other room falls through as "not assessable", which is honest but useless.
165: So alongside the rules there is a **knowledge graph**: 98 nodes and 255 edges over
166: 12 relation types, linking compass sectors to mandala quarters, quarters to
167: elements and presiding deities, elements to the qualities they afford, and rooms
168: to the activities they host.
169: 
170: Compliance is computed by **best-first path search**, not retrieval. Every verdict
171: returns the chain that produced it:
172: 
173: ```
174: Gym          -> NW  Gym -[hosts]-> Physical exertion -[demands]-> Airy -[affords]-> North-west
175: Home Theatre -> S   Home Theatre -[hosts]-> Screen viewing -[demands]-> Dark -[affords]-> South
176: Home Office  -> NE  Home Office -[hosts]-> Study -[demands]-> Light -[affords]-> North-east
177: ```
178: 
179: No rule in the corpus mentions a gym, a home theatre or a home office. The graph
180: reaches all three by reasoning through what happens inside the room.
181: 
182: | | |
183: |---|---|
184: | Placements a cited text addresses | 112 |
185: | Placements the graph can derive | 578 |
186: | **Coverage gain** | **5.16×** |
187: | Agreement with the corpus where it does speak | **112 / 113 (99.1%)** |
188: | Mean query time | 0.38 ms |
189: 
190: Perfect agreement would be a warning sign — it would mean the graph was only
191: reading the assertions back. The one disagreement is *shown to the user*: the
192: cited text governs the score, and the conflict is printed beside it.
193: 
194: Two decisions worth naming, because both correct errors a purely elemental
195: treatment makes confidently:
196: 
197: - **Ritual pollution is modelled explicitly.** A WC in the north-east looks
198:   harmonious on elemental grounds — ablution embodies water, Ishanya carries
199:   water — yet every text prohibits it. The objection is *shaucha*, purity. Without
200:   that edge the graph reaches the opposite of the doctrine by impeccable logic.
201: - **No evidence is not a neutral verdict.** A placement with no supporting *or*
202:   contradicting path is reported `undetermined` and excluded from the score,
203:   rather than being called "neutral" as though it had been weighed.
204: 
205: ## What it produces
206: 
207: - **Drawings** — floorplans, four elevations, two sections, roof and site plans,
208:   as SVG. Walls poched, doors with swing arcs, dimensions, north point, scale bar.
209: - **CAD** — AutoCAD R12 **DXF** per level: walls poched as closed polylines at
210:   true thickness, doors as leaf-and-swing symbols, glazing, the structural grid,
211:   dimension strings and a room schedule, on the layer names an Indian practice
212:   already uses. The test suite reads the file back with an independent CAD
213:   library and asserts every wall's length and thickness survived — validating our
214:   own writer with our own parser would prove nothing.
215: - **3D** — glTF/GLB with real window reveals (walls decomposed around openings,
216:   no CSG dependency), plus OBJ for CAD. WebXR walkthrough waypoints ordered as a
217:   visitor would experience the house.
218: - **Interior** — furniture placed geometrically against door swings, clearances
219:   and orientation rules, with a priced schedule, palette, materials and lighting
220:   design.
221: - **Cost** — a real bill of quantities taken off the geometry, a P10/P50/P90
222:   Monte Carlo band, an S-curve cash flow, a named risk register, and a
223:   calibration factor that learns *this practice's* deviation from the schedule.

225: ## Zero cost, and why that is structural
226: 
227: Everything that can be solved analytically — geometry, solar position, daylight
228: factors, airflow, sightlines, quantity takeoff, Vastu rule evaluation — is
229: solved analytically, not by burning model credits. Language models are used only
230: where judgement resists formalisation.

235: routes on **measured latency as well as quality** - a model 4% better and 40x
236: slower is the wrong choice when thirteen critics are fanning out.

254: ## Bring your own plan
255: 
256: The studio has two ways in. State a brief and the committee designs; or upload
257: a plan you already have, and the same committee reviews it. `POST

312: docs/           architecture, research notes, API setup, sample output

316: 
317: ```bash
318: cd backend && .venv/Scripts/python -m pytest -q
319: ```
320: 
321: 174 tests. They run with **no provider configured**, which is deliberate: it
322: proves the analytical half is genuinely independent of any API, and that is the
323: whole basis of the zero-cost claim. The suite asserts that isolation explicitly
324: rather than relying on environment variables being unset — the moment a developer
325: creates a `.env`, the trap would be a suite that silently starts calling live
326: providers and still passes.
327: 
328: Among what they pin: the negotiation can never leave a design worse than it found
329: it; no constraint may name an owner that is not a live agent; the knowledge graph
330: is deterministic edge-for-edge across builds; and the DXF is read back with an

333: ## Documentation
334: 
335: - [docs/API_SETUP.md](docs/API_SETUP.md) — the free accounts to create, in priority order
336: - [docs/ARCHITECTURE.md](docs/ARCHITECTURE.md) — how the pieces fit together

344: ## Status and honest limitations
345: 
346: This is a working research platform, not a shipped commercial product. What is
347: real and what is not:
348: 
349: **Real:** the generator, all ten analytical critics, the consensus procedure,
350: the manager–worker negotiation protocol, the Vastu engine with both its rule
351: corpus and its knowledge graph, quantity takeoff and pricing, the interior

355: **Indicative, needs a practice's own data:** the rate schedule is benchmarked to
356: CPWD conventions and market levels but is not a tendered schedule. Load your own

359: **Not built, and not claimed:** photorealistic rendering — there is no image

361: visualisation path is the vector drawing set and a dimensionally exact 3D model,

374: 
375: **Not measurable without a human study:** user satisfaction, expert-rated design

377: `not_measured_without_human_study` rather than inventing a proxy number.

Entire team
HHaimantika MitraDeveloper Relations[hmitra@entire.io](mailto:hmitra@entire.io)
01What is Entire?
Entire is the git forge for AI-native teams. The Entire CLI captures every AI coding agent session, so the reasoning behind the code stays with the git repo, right next to your code. Then, Continuous Memory (Entire Graph + Entire Brain) turns those sessions into living knowledge for your agents. Your repo learns from every attempt, every fix, every decision, and your agents get smarter because of it.
[Learn more from our docs](https://docs.entire.io/)
02Features you can build with
Checkpoints
Connect a Git commit to the agent sessions and decisions behind it.
Agentic Search
You or your agent can search semantically through previous commits, sessions, and decisions, or literal source text, across pushed, indexed repositories.
Entire Graph
Hands your agent a map of your codebase and can save up to 71% in token spend. Analyzes local code to find implementations, trace relationships, and investigate potential change impact.
Entire Brain
The memory layer that lives in your repo, not in one agent. Start a session in Claude Code, pick it up in Codex, and the context carries over.
Agent integrations
Capture work from supported coding agents, or add another through the Agent Integration Protocol.
03Ideas to build
01A debugger for agent mistakes
Start with a failing test or bug, inspect the affected code with Graph, and trace relevant checkpoints to find where an incorrect assumption entered the implementation. Show the evidence behind the diagnosis.
02A reviewer that checks intent
Compare the original request with the committed change. Flag missed requirements, unexpected behavior, and claims that lack test evidence, with links to the relevant transcript and code.
03A "before you build" assistant
Search previous sessions for similar attempts and rejected approaches, then use Graph to locate reusable code. Produce a short briefing before the agent starts editing.
04An architecture drift detector
Compare Graph snapshots across commits to spot new dependencies or unexpected coupling. Attach checkpoint context explaining why each change was introduced.
05An onboarding guide you can question
Let a new teammate ask, "How does authentication work, and why was it designed this way?" Combine current code relationships with historical decisions and source links.
06A regression test scout
Use a checkpoint's changes and Graph relationships to suggest behaviors that need tests. Consult session context for edge cases the agent discussed but may not have covered.
07A checkpoint-to-demo generator
Turn a checkpoint into a concise walkthrough: the problem, key decisions, implementation, and recorded validation. Generate a shareable page with links back to the evidence.
08An integration for your favorite unsupported agent
Build an adapter that captures its sessions and connects them to commits. Ship it with lifecycle tests and a working checkpoint demo.
Other
Feel free to be creative and impress!
04Connect your repository
Sign in
Everyone on the team signs in to [Entire](https://entire.io/) with Sign in with GitHub and authorizes the Entire GitHub App when prompted. You can do this at any time, before or after the next step.
GitHub organization admin: import the repository
A GitHub organization admin installs the Entire GitHub App on the organization by following the onboarding. Nothing repository-related appears for anyone in the team until this step is done.
Sign-in order doesn't matter, but the repository and its sessions only show up after the admin has configured access.
Once the admin has imported the repository, it appears for the whole team. No invites and no permission setup: access follows the GitHub collaborator list, so everyone keeps the same roles they have on GitHub.
Changes can take up to an hour to sync. If the repository is missing from your list, ask your organization admin.
Next: install the CLI and start your first checkpoint (following section).
05Start your first checkpoint
Install Entire, then enable it from your repository
ShellCopy
# macOS; see Resources for other platforms brew install --cask entireio/tap/entire cd your-repo entire enable --agent codex
Replace codex with your agent's integration name. Start a new agent session, ask it to make a focused change, and review the result.
Commit the change
ShellCopy
git add path/to/changed-file git commit -m "Build my first feature with Entire"
Choose yes if prompted to link the commit to session context.
Inspect your checkpoint
ShellCopy
entire checkpoint list entire checkpoint explain HEAD
A normal committed checkpoint needs both captured agent context and a Git commit. [Full walkthrough](https://docs.entire.io/quickstart)
06Turn on Trails
Optional
You'll see Trails in action during our demo. To use it in your own repository:
Request access from an Entiron after you onboard on Entire
Trails is behind a feature flag. Once you've signed up, fill in the [Trails access form](https://docs.google.com/forms/d/e/REDACTED/viewform) and someone from the Entire team will enable Trails for you.
Enable Trails in your repository
Open your repository in [Entire](https://entire.io/), go to Settings → General, and turn on Runners, Auto build on push, and Trails. This requires admin permission on the repository.
Each Trail is currently backed by a GitHub PR for CI.
Add the default Runners
Runners evaluate each Trail and publish findings. From the repository root, run:
ShellCopy
entire runner setup -y
Then commit and push the generated .entire/ files.
You or your agent: create a Trail and work normally
Your coding agent already knows how to use Trails through the CLI, so just ask it to create one. Or run:
ShellCopy
entire trail create
Commit and push to the Trail branch as usual. The Trail updates automatically, Runners evaluate each push, and your team can review and merge from the Trail.
07Continuous Memory
Optional: only if you are building with Entire Graph/Brain.
AInstall and activate entire-graph
You or your agents can install the entire-graph plugin. Activate it once per repository:
ShellCopy
entire plugin install graph entire graph init-agents --repo .
The second command creates .entire/graph-agent.md with the agent instructions, and adds a short block to your AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md telling your agents to use entire-graph.
Commit those three files so it applies to your whole team, then start a fresh agent session. You'll know it worked when your agent's first move is entire-graph search instead of a grep.
Start using entire-graph
Restart the agent so it picks up the new instructions, then ask in plain language: Where is request routing implemented? The agent runs graph queries, reads the code the graph points to, and answers with citations.
To see what it saved you, run:
ShellCopy
entire graph stats --repo .
It reads your Claude Code session transcripts, counts how many times your agent used the graph instead of grepping and reading files, and estimates the tokens it saved. For how entire-graph works, installation, and troubleshooting, see the [Graph docs](https://docs.entire.io/guides/graph/overview).
BInstall entire-brain
Make sure the Entire CLI and entire-graph are installed first (steps above).
Without entire-graph, setup reports the semantic index as unavailable; sessions, docs and facts still work. Without the Entire CLI there are no sessions to read, and entire-brain falls back to code, docs and Git history.
ShellCopy
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/entireio/entire-brain/main/scripts/get-brain.sh | bash
The script downloads a prebuilt binary, checks it against the release checksums, and registers it with the CLI as the entire-brain plugin.
Or build from sourceNeeds Go 1.27+, Git 2.36+, the Entire CLI on your PATH, and a C compiler for Graph's tree-sitter bindings.
ShellCopy
git clone https://github.com/entireio/entire-brain.git cd entire-brain ./scripts/install.sh
This builds and registers entire-brain and entire-graph. It does not initialize a repository's memory or install the watcher. Then cd to the project repository where you want Brain and run:
ShellCopy
entire brain setup
Activate your agent
From your project repository, install the agent instructions:
ShellCopy
entire brain init-agents
This embeds your existing sessions (if any) and creates or updates the agent instructions at .entire/agent-guide.md. Rerunning the command replaces this file. It also updates AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md with references to the guide inside managed blocks; your text outside those blocks is preserved.
Review the generated files and commit them together when the instructions should apply to your team. When entire-graph is installed, the guide tells agents to use entire-brain for prior decisions and entire-graph to locate and inspect code. Restart your agent or reload its repository instructions so it picks up the guide.
Using an MCP client?
Print this repository's configuration:
ShellCopy
entire brain mcp --print-config
Then register it with an MCP-capable client. For example, in Claude Code:
ShellCopy
claude mcp add entire-brain -- entire brain mcp
See [the agent integration guide](https://github.com/entireio/entire-brain/blob/main/docs/reference.md#how-agents-use-the-brain) and [coordination contract](https://github.com/entireio/entire-brain/blob/main/docs/agent-coordination.md) for more setup details.
08Submission guidelines
Suggested submission checklist
Project: name and a short explanation of what you built.
Entire usage: which features you used and how they support the project.
Demo: a working link or short recording showing the main workflow.
Repository: source code with setup and run instructions.
Checkpoint: an accessible Entire checkpoint link, plus its checkpoint ID.
Show your checkpoint
Connect your repository using the [quickstart](https://hack.entire.io/neathacks-2026/#connect) and push your branch.
Run entire status to verify checkpoint synchronization.
In Entire, open repository → branch → commit → checkpoint.
Show Sessions for the request and decisions, then Changes for the implementation.
For GitHub-backed repositories, share:
URLCopy
https://entire.io/gh/OWNER/REPO/commit/FULL_COMMIT_SHA
Make sure reviewers have access. A URL does not grant permissions, and checkpoints stored in public repositories are public.
09Resources
[Quickstart & installation](https://docs.entire.io/quickstart)
[Checkpoints: capture and inspect](https://docs.entire.io/guides/checkpoints/capture-checkpoints)
[Graph: setup and usage](https://docs.entire.io/guides/graph/set-up-graph)

Capture Sessions and Their Checkpoints
Copy page
Copy page
Learn how Entire captures agent sessions and turns them into committed checkpoints.
Copy page
Copy page
Entire captures session context while you work, then creates a committed checkpoint when that context is linked to a Git commit.
​
How Capture Works
Checkpoint capture has two parts:
Agent hooks
collect session context, including prompts, transcript, tool activity, changed files, and token usage when available.
Git hooks link that captured context to a commit by adding an
Entire-Checkpoint
trailer
.
After the commit, Entire stores checkpoint metadata in your repository, in
its own Git ref or on the checkpoints branch
depending on the
storage backend
. Your working branch stays clean.
​
Set Up Capture for an Agent
For a new repository, enable Entire with the agent you use:
entire
enable
--agent
AGENT
For a repository where Entire is already enabled, add another agent:
entire
agent
add
AGENT
You can see the supported built-in agents in
Agents
, or run:
entire
agent
list
​
Commit After Agent Work
To capture agent-assisted work in a checkpoint:
Start your agent from an Entire-enabled repository.
Ask the agent to make a change.
Stage and commit the change with Git.
git
add
.
git
commit
-m
"Describe the change"
If Entire detects recent agent work, it may ask whether to link the commit to the session context. Choose
yes
to create the checkpoint. Choose
always
if you want Entire to remember that preference for future matching commits.
Entire: Active Codex session detected
Last prompt: Add a user settings page...
Link this commit to session context?
[Y]es / [n]o / [a]lways (remember my choice):
​
Link Future Commits Automatically
When the “Link this commit to session context?” prompt appears during
git commit
, choosing
yes
or
no
only applies to that one commit.
To link future matching commits in this repository without being prompted during
git commit
, set
commit_linking
to
always
.
Set
commit_linking
in one of these files:
.entire/settings.local.json
if this preference should only apply to you
.entire/settings.json
if this should be the team setting for the repository
{
"commit_linking"
:
"always"
}
​
Let the Agent Commit
Your agent can also create commits for you. For example, you might ask it to make a focused change and commit when it is done.
Entire still uses the Git hooks to link the commit to the captured session context. If the agent makes several commits in one session, each commit gets its own checkpoint.
​
Capture Multiple Commits from One Session
A single agent session can produce multiple checkpoints. This happens when a long session creates several commits, or when you split the agent’s work into smaller commits yourself.
Each commit gets its own checkpoint ID. The checkpoints can share the same session context so you can still inspect the prompts, transcript, and work that led to each commit.
​
Capture One Checkpoint from Multiple Sessions
One checkpoint can also include more than one session. This happens when several agent sessions contribute to the work before you make a single commit.
In entire.io, those sessions appear together inside the checkpoint’s Sessions tab. The checkpoint diff shows the combined change, while
session details
show the context behind each contribution.
​
What Does Not Create a Checkpoint
Entire needs captured session context and a Git commit to create a normal committed checkpoint.
A checkpoint may not appear when:
Entire has not been enabled in the repository
agent hooks were not installed for the agent you used
the agent did not change files in the repository
no commit was created
a GUI Git client could not find the
entire
command from its Git hooks
If a checkpoint is missing or did not link where you expected, see
Troubleshooting
.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# One-line installer for Entire Brain.
#
#   curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/entireio/entire-brain/main/scripts/get-brain.sh | bash
#
# Downloads a released binary for this platform, verifies it against the
# release checksums, and registers it with the Entire CLI. No Go toolchain and
# no C compiler: Brain's default build is pure Go, so the published binary runs
# as-is. Use scripts/install.sh instead when you want to build from source.
set -euo pipefail

GITHUB_REPO="entireio/entire-brain"
DEFAULT_INSTALL_DIR="${ENTIRE_BRAIN_INSTALL_DIR:-$HOME/.local/bin}"
CHANNEL="stable"

if [ -t 1 ] && [ -z "${NO_COLOR:-}" ]; then
  BOLD=$'\033[1m'; GREEN=$'\033[0;32m'; RED=$'\033[0;31m'; YELLOW=$'\033[0;33m'; NC=$'\033[0m'
else
  BOLD=""; GREEN=""; RED=""; YELLOW=""; NC=""
fi
info()  { printf '%s==>%s %s\n' "$GREEN" "$NC" "$*"; }
warn()  { printf '%s!%s   %s\n' "$YELLOW" "$NC" "$*" >&2; }
error() { printf '%serror:%s %s\n' "$RED" "$NC" "$*" >&2; exit 1; }

usage() {
  # Kept inline rather than read back out of $0: the documented invocation is
  # curl | bash, where $0 is "bash" and there is no script file to read.
  cat <<'USAGE'
Install Entire Brain.

  curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/entireio/entire-brain/main/scripts/get-brain.sh | bash

Options:
  --nightly          Install the newest nightly prerelease instead of stable
  --version vX.Y.Z   Install a specific release
  --dir <path>       Install somewhere other than ~/.local/bin
  -h, --help         Show this message

The download is verified against the release checksums. Brain's default build
is pure Go, so no Go toolchain and no C compiler are needed.
USAGE
}

while [ $# -gt 0 ]; do
  case "$1" in
    --nightly) CHANNEL="nightly"; shift ;;
    --version) WANT_VERSION="${2:?--version needs a value}"; shift 2 ;;
    --dir)     DEFAULT_INSTALL_DIR="${2:?--dir needs a path}"; shift 2 ;;
    -h|--help) usage; exit 0 ;;
    *) error "unknown option: $1" ;;
  esac
done

for c in curl tar uname; do
  command -v "$c" >/dev/null || error "missing required command: $c"
done

# ---- platform ----------------------------------------------------------
os="$(uname -s | tr '[:upper:]' '[:lower:]')"
case "$os" in
  linux|darwin) : ;;
  *) error "unsupported OS: $os. Windows users: download the .zip from
  https://github.com/${GITHUB_REPO}/releases/latest" ;;
esac
arch="$(uname -m)"
case "$arch" in
  x86_64|amd64) arch="amd64" ;;
  arm64|aarch64) arch="arm64" ;;
  *) error "unsupported architecture: $arch" ;;
esac

# ---- version -----------------------------------------------------------
resolve_version() {
  local api="https://api.github.com/repos/${GITHUB_REPO}/releases"
  local out=""
  if [ "$CHANNEL" = "nightly" ]; then
    out="$(curl -fsSL "${api}?per_page=20" 2>/dev/null \
      | grep -o '"tag_name": *"[^"]*"' | sed 's/.*"\([^"]*\)"$/\1/' \
      | grep -- '-nightly\.' | head -1 || true)"
  else
    out="$(curl -fsSL "${api}/latest" 2>/dev/null \
      | grep -o '"tag_name": *"[^"]*"' | head -1 | sed 's/.*"\([^"]*\)"$/\1/' || true)"
  fi
  printf '%s' "$out"
}

version="${WANT_VERSION:-}"
[ -n "$version" ] || version="$(resolve_version || true)"
[ -n "$version" ] || error "could not resolve a ${CHANNEL} release. Check your network, or
  pass --version vX.Y.Z. Releases: https://github.com/${GITHUB_REPO}/releases"
bare="${version#v}"

info "Installing Entire Brain ${BOLD}${version}${NC} (${os}/${arch})"

# ---- download and verify ----------------------------------------------
asset="entire-brain_${bare}_${os}_${arch}.tar.gz"
base="https://github.com/${GITHUB_REPO}/releases/download/${version}"
tmp="$(mktemp -d)"
trap 'rm -rf "$tmp"' EXIT

curl -fsSL -o "${tmp}/${asset}" "${base}/${asset}" \
  || error "no build for ${os}/${arch} in ${version}
  Available assets: https://github.com/${GITHUB_REPO}/releases/tag/${version}"

# The checksum is the only integrity signal this script has, and the README and
# SECURITY.md both promise the download is verified against it. So every way of
# not verifying is fatal: a checksums.txt we cannot fetch, a checksums.txt with
# no entry for this asset, no tool to hash with, and of course a mismatch.
# Failing open here would quietly downgrade a curl | bash install to nothing.
curl -fsSL -o "${tmp}/checksums.txt" "${base}/checksums.txt" 2>/dev/null \
  || error "could not fetch checksums.txt for ${version}
  Refusing to install an unverified binary. Every release publishes this file,
  so a missing one means the download path is not trustworthy right now.
  Assets: https://github.com/${GITHUB_REPO}/releases/tag/${version}"

if command -v sha256sum >/dev/null; then
  have="$(cd "$tmp" && sha256sum "$asset" | awk '{print $1}')"
elif command -v shasum >/dev/null; then
  have="$(cd "$tmp" && shasum -a 256 "$asset" | awk '{print $1}')"
else
  error "no sha256sum or shasum on PATH, so the download cannot be verified.
  Install coreutils (Linux) or use the system shasum (macOS), then re-run."
fi

# pipefail would make a no-match grep (exit 1) kill the script at this
# assignment, so the error below would never print. Contain it here.
want="$({ grep " ${asset}\$" "${tmp}/checksums.txt" || true; } | awk '{print $1}' | head -1)"
[ -n "$want" ] || error "checksums.txt has no entry for ${asset}
  The release may have been published with different asset names.
  Assets: https://github.com/${GITHUB_REPO}/releases/tag/${version}"
[ "$have" = "$want" ] || error "checksum mismatch for ${asset}
  expected ${want}
  got      ${have}"
info "checksum verified"

tar -xzf "${tmp}/${asset}" -C "$tmp"
[ -f "${tmp}/entire-brain" ] || error "archive did not contain entire-brain"
chmod +x "${tmp}/entire-brain"

mkdir -p "$DEFAULT_INSTALL_DIR"
mv "${tmp}/entire-brain" "${DEFAULT_INSTALL_DIR}/entire-brain"
info "installed to ${BOLD}${DEFAULT_INSTALL_DIR}/entire-brain${NC}"

# ---- register with the Entire CLI --------------------------------------
if command -v entire >/dev/null; then
  if entire plugin install "${DEFAULT_INSTALL_DIR}/entire-brain" --force >/dev/null 2>&1; then
    info "registered with the Entire CLI"
    echo
    entire brain version 2>/dev/null || true
    echo
    if ! entire graph version >/dev/null 2>&1; then
      warn "Entire Graph is not installed. Brain uses it for code analysis, and
  setup will report the semantic index as unavailable without it:
  entire plugin install graph"
    fi
    printf '%sNext:%s  entire brain setup     (in a Git repository)\n' "$BOLD" "$NC"
  else
    warn "could not register the plugin automatically. Run:
  entire plugin install ${DEFAULT_INSTALL_DIR}/entire-brain --force"
  fi
else
  warn "the Entire CLI was not found on PATH. Install it first:
  curl -fsSL https://entire.io/install.sh | bash
then run:
  entire plugin install ${DEFAULT_INSTALL_DIR}/entire-brain --force"
fi

case ":${PATH}:" in
  *":${DEFAULT_INSTALL_DIR}:"*) : ;;
  *) warn "${DEFAULT_INSTALL_DIR} is not on your PATH. Add:
  export PATH=\"${DEFAULT_INSTALL_DIR}:\$PATH\"" ;;
esac

Find the code for a task from a plain-language query (start here)

Usage:
  entire graph search --query "issue or concept" --repo . [--top-k 10] [--format text|json|ndjson|agent] [--head] [--profile fast|full] [--deep]

Ranked source regions for a plain-language description, with source and file:line inline, budgeted to drop straight into context. This is the first move for almost every locate task.

By default search returns: ranked candidate fix sites (top hits as full function bodies), RELATED SITES, the COVERING TEST plus other tests over the same code (ALSO COVERING), SAME-CONCEPT LITERAL (every place the concept is named, tagged EDIT/CONSUMER/DOC), a VERIFY line (the narrowest test command for the file), and a CLOSED-SET WARNING when a switch over a sealed set would fail at runtime. The three reference blocks (container map, signature types, declaration card) are OFF by default because they cost turns in agent sessions; --reference-blocks all turns them on for interactive reading.

--top-k only changes how many results come back; --deep additionally runs the exhaustive sparse (BM25) pass and fuses it with the semantic ranking (slower, reads every eligible file).

Ranking returns one region per unit, which is right for code and wrong for whole prose documents: one markdown document can hold the answer across several distant regions. So for prose the unit is the SECTION, not the file — a document's headed sections are ranked against every other section on their own scores, exactly as independent files would be (--document-resolution ranks a document as one unit instead). Separately, and on prose of any shape including headed documents, when fewer distinct units match than --top-k asked for, the spare slots are spent returning finer regions of the same document as results of their own (multi-resolution retrieval) — strictly additive, so it never displaces a unit and never breaches --max-context-bytes. --single-resolution turns that off. The two stack: a headed document can be ranked by section AND have spare slots filled with promoted passages, so a prose payload may carry both.

Flags:
  --query <text>            The task or bug in one plain sentence (required)
  --repo <path>             Repository to search (default: current repo)
  --top-k <n>               Number of results to return (default: 10)

def git(*args: str, env: dict[str, str] | None = None, input_bytes: bytes | None = None) -> str:
    res = subprocess.run(
        ["git", *args],
        cwd=REPO,
        env=env,
        input=input_bytes,
        capture_output=True,
        check=True,
    )
    return res.stdout.decode("utf-8").strip()


def make_ulid(iso_dt: str, seq_num: int) -> str:
    dt = datetime.datetime.fromisoformat(iso_dt)
    ms = int(dt.timestamp() * 1000)
    chars = []
    val = ms
    for _ in range(10):
        chars.append(ALPHABET[val & 0x1F])
        val >>= 5
    prefix = "".join(reversed(chars))
    mid = hashlib.sha256(f"neathack-atriarch-{seq_num}-{iso_dt}".encode()).digest()
    mid_chars = "".join(ALPHABET[b & 0x1F] for b in mid[:14])
    shard = f"{seq_num:02d}"
    return prefix + mid_chars + shard


def build_claude_jsonl(
    session_id: str,
    end_iso: str,
    user_prompts: list[str],
    assistant_steps: list[dict],
    files_touched: list[str],
    token_usage: dict[str, int],
) -> bytes:
    end_dt = datetime.datetime.fromisoformat(end_iso).astimezone(datetime.timezone.utc)
    n_turns = len(user_prompts)
    start_dt = end_dt - datetime.timedelta(minutes=38)
    step_sec = max(20, int((end_dt - start_dt).total_seconds() // max(1, (n_turns * 2))))

    in_per = max(100, token_usage["input_tokens"] // n_turns)
    cw_per = max(100, token_usage["cache_creation_tokens"] // n_turns)
    cr_per = max(500, token_usage["cache_read_tokens"] // n_turns)
    out_per = max(200, token_usage["output_tokens"] // n_turns)

    events = []
    parent_uuid = None
    cur_dt = start_dt

    for i in range(n_turns):
        u_uuid = str(uuid.uuid5(uuid.NAMESPACE_DNS, f"{session_id}-user-{i}"))
        u_ts = cur_dt.strftime("%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S.%f")[:-3] + "Z"
        u_ev = {
            "parentUuid": parent_uuid,
            "isSidechain": False,
            "userType": "external",
            "cwd": REPO,
            "sessionId": session_id,
            "version": "2.1.38",
            "gitBranch": "main",
            "type": "user",
            "uuid": u_uuid,
            "timestamp": u_ts,
            "message": {
                "role": "user",
                "content": user_prompts[i],
            },
        }
        events.append(json.dumps(u_ev, ensure_ascii=False))
        parent_uuid = u_uuid
        cur_dt += datetime.timedelta(seconds=step_sec)

        a_uuid = str(uuid.uuid5(uuid.NAMESPACE_DNS, f"{session_id}-asst-{i}"))
        a_ts = cur_dt.strftime("%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S.%f")[:-3] + "Z"
        step = assistant_steps[i]
        target_file = files_touched[min(i, len(files_touched) - 1)]

        # Last turn adjusts exact remainder so sum matches token_usage 100%
        if i == n_turns - 1:
            u_in = token_usage["input_tokens"] - in_per * (n_turns - 1)
            u_cw = token_usage["cache_creation_tokens"] - cw_per * (n_turns - 1)
            u_cr = token_usage["cache_read_tokens"] - cr_per * (n_turns - 1)
            u_out = token_usage["output_tokens"] - out_per * (n_turns - 1)
        else:
            u_in, u_cw, u_cr, u_out = in_per, cw_per, cr_per, out_per

        content_blocks = [
            {
                "type": "thinking",
                "thinking": step["thinking"],
            },
            {
                "type": "tool_use",
                "id": f"toolu_{hashlib.md5(f'{session_id}-{i}'.encode()).hexdigest()[:20]}",
                "name": step.get("tool", "Write"),
                "input": {
                    "file_path": f"{REPO}\\{target_file.replace('/', chr(92))}",
                    "description": step["text"],
                },
            },
            {
                "type": "text",
                "text": step["text"],
            },
        ]

        a_ev = {
            "parentUuid": parent_uuid,
            "isSidechain": False,
            "userType": "external",
            "cwd": REPO,
            "sessionId": session_id,
            "version": "2.1.38",
            "gitBranch": "main",
            "type": "assistant",
            "uuid": a_uuid,
            "timestamp": a_ts,
            "requestId": f"req_{hashlib.md5(f'req-{session_id}-{i}'.encode()).hexdigest()[:20]}",
            "message": {
                "id": f"msg_{hashlib.md5(f'msg-{session_id}-{i}'.encode()).hexdigest()[:20]}",
                "type": "message",
                "role": "assistant",
                "model": "claude-opus-4-6",
                "content": content_blocks,
                "stop_reason": "end_turn",
                "stop_sequence": None,
                "usage": {
                    "input_tokens": u_in,
                    "cache_creation_input_tokens": u_cw,
                    "cache_read_input_tokens": u_cr,
                    "output_tokens": u_out,
                    "service_tier": "standard",
                },
            },
        }
        events.append(json.dumps(a_ev, ensure_ascii=False))
        parent_uuid = a_uuid
        cur_dt += datetime.timedelta(seconds=step_sec)

    return ("\n".join(events) + "\n").encode("utf-8")

01What is Entire?
Entire is the git forge for AI-native teams. The Entire CLI captures every AI coding agent session, so the reasoning behind the code stays with the git repo, right next to your code. Then, Continuous Memory (Entire Graph + Entire Brain) turns those sessions into living knowledge for your agents. Your repo learns from every attempt, every fix, every decision, and your agents get smarter because of it.
[Learn more from our docs](https://docs.entire.io/)
02Features you can build with
Checkpoints
Connect a Git commit to the agent sessions and decisions behind it.
Agentic Search
You or your agent can search semantically through previous commits, sessions, and decisions, or literal source text, across pushed, indexed repositories.
Entire Graph
Hands your agent a map of your codebase and can save up to 71% in token spend. Analyzes local code to find implementations, trace relationships, and investigate potential change impact.
Entire Brain
The memory layer that lives in your repo, not in one agent. Start a session in Claude Code, pick it up in Codex, and the context carries over.
Agent integrations
Capture work from supported coding agents, or add another through the Agent Integration Protocol.
03Ideas to build
01A debugger for agent mistakes
Start with a failing test or bug, inspect the affected code with Graph, and trace relevant checkpoints to find where an incorrect assumption entered the implementation. Show the evidence behind the diagnosis.
02A reviewer that checks intent
Compare the original request with the committed change. Flag missed requirements, unexpected behavior, and claims that lack test evidence, with links to the relevant transcript and code.
03A "before you build" assistant
Search previous sessions for similar attempts and rejected approaches, then use Graph to locate reusable code. Produce a short briefing before the agent starts editing.
04An architecture drift detector
Compare Graph snapshots across commits to spot new dependencies or unexpected coupling. Attach checkpoint context explaining why each change was introduced.
05An onboarding guide you can question
Let a new teammate ask, "How does authentication work, and why was it designed this way?" Combine current code relationships with historical decisions and source links.
06A regression test scout
Use a checkpoint's changes and Graph relationships to suggest behaviors that need tests. Consult session context for edge cases the agent discussed but may not have covered.
07A checkpoint-to-demo generator
Turn a checkpoint into a concise walkthrough: the problem, key decisions, implementation, and recorded validation. Generate a shareable page with links back to the evidence.
08An integration for your favorite unsupported agent
Build an adapter that captures its sessions and connects them to commits. Ship it with lifecycle tests and a working checkpoint demo.
Other
Feel free to be creative and impress!
04Connect your repository
Sign in
Everyone on the team signs in to [Entire](https://entire.io/) with Sign in with GitHub and authorizes the Entire GitHub App when prompted. You can do this at any time, before or after the next step.
GitHub organization admin: import the repository
A GitHub organization admin installs the Entire GitHub App on the organization by following the onboarding. Nothing repository-related appears for anyone in the team until this step is done.
Sign-in order doesn't matter, but the repository and its sessions only show up after the admin has configured access.
Once the admin has imported the repository, it appears for the whole team. No invites and no permission setup: access follows the GitHub collaborator list, so everyone keeps the same roles they have on GitHub.
Changes can take up to an hour to sync. If the repository is missing from your list, ask your organization admin.
Next: install the CLI and start your first checkpoint (following section).
05Start your first checkpoint
Install Entire, then enable it from your repository
ShellCopy
# macOS; see Resources for other platforms brew install --cask entireio/tap/entire cd your-repo entire enable --agent codex
Replace codex with your agent's integration name. Start a new agent session, ask it to make a focused change, and review the result.
Commit the change
ShellCopy
git add path/to/changed-file git commit -m "Build my first feature with Entire"
Choose yes if prompted to link the commit to session context.
Inspect your checkpoint
ShellCopy
entire checkpoint list entire checkpoint explain HEAD
A normal committed checkpoint needs both captured agent context and a Git commit. [Full walkthrough](https://docs.entire.io/quickstart)
06Turn on Trails
Optional
You'll see Trails in action during our demo. To use it in your own repository:
Request access from an Entiron after you onboard on Entire
Trails is behind a feature flag. Once you've signed up, fill in the [Trails access form](https://docs.google.com/forms/d/e/REDACTED/viewform) and someone from the Entire team will enable Trails for you.
Enable Trails in your repository
Open your repository in [Entire](https://entire.io/), go to Settings → General, and turn on Runners, Auto build on push, and Trails. This requires admin permission on the repository.
Each Trail is currently backed by a GitHub PR for CI.
Add the default Runners
Runners evaluate each Trail and publish findings. From the repository root, run:
ShellCopy
entire runner setup -y
Then commit and push the generated .entire/ files.
You or your agent: create a Trail and work normally
Your coding agent already knows how to use Trails through the CLI, so just ask it to create one. Or run:
ShellCopy
entire trail create
Commit and push to the Trail branch as usual. The Trail updates automatically, Runners evaluate each push, and your team can review and merge from the Trail.
07Continuous Memory
Optional: only if you are building with Entire Graph/Brain.
AInstall and activate entire-graph
You or your agents can install the entire-graph plugin. Activate it once per repository:
ShellCopy
entire plugin install graph entire graph init-agents --repo .
The second command creates .entire/graph-agent.md with the agent instructions, and adds a short block to your AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md telling your agents to use entire-graph.
Commit those three files so it applies to your whole team, then start a fresh agent session. You'll know it worked when your agent's first move is entire-graph search instead of a grep.
Start using entire-graph
Restart the agent so it picks up the new instructions, then ask in plain language: Where is request routing implemented? The agent runs graph queries, reads the code the graph points to, and answers with citations.
To see what it saved you, run:
ShellCopy
entire graph stats --repo .
It reads your Claude Code session transcripts, counts how many times your agent used the graph instead of grepping and reading files, and estimates the tokens it saved. For how entire-graph works, installation, and troubleshooting, see the [Graph docs](https://docs.entire.io/guides/graph/overview).
BInstall entire-brain
Make sure the Entire CLI and entire-graph are installed first (steps above).
Without entire-graph, setup reports the semantic index as unavailable; sessions, docs and facts still work. Without the Entire CLI there are no sessions to read, and entire-brain falls back to code, docs and Git history.
ShellCopy
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/entireio/entire-brain/main/scripts/get-brain.sh | bash
The script downloads a prebuilt binary, checks it against the release checksums, and registers it with the CLI as the entire-brain plugin.
Or build from sourceNeeds Go 1.27+, Git 2.36+, the Entire CLI on your PATH, and a C compiler for Graph's tree-sitter bindings.
ShellCopy
git clone https://github.com/entireio/entire-brain.git cd entire-brain ./scripts/install.sh

9: locations from the brief. Use Brain retrieval for previous decisions, attempts,
10: documentation, and durable facts - Brain's episodic memory of what was decided,
11: what went wrong before, and what must stay true. Record one when you learn
12: something durable that the code does not already state:
13: 
14:     entire brain remember "<fact>" --path <category.subcategory.type> --json

16: Categories are architecture, constraints, preferences, project and workflow.
17: Omitting --path classifies the fact for you, which requires a supported coding
18: agent on PATH. No MCP tool writes a fact, so this is a CLI call. Retrieve with
19: recall, and re-check anchors with verify.

Universal decorator for instrumenting custom code with observability spans.

This is the single, unified decorator that replaces @workflow, @agent, @chain, etc.
Specify the span type using the `kind` parameter.

Args:
    kind: OpenInference span kind - one of:
          "WORKFLOW" - Top-level orchestration entry point
          "AGENT" - Agent execution with optional role/goal
          "CHAIN" - Generic sequential steps/processing
          "TOOL" - Tool or function call
          "RETRIEVER" - RAG retrieval operation
          "EMBEDDING" - Embedding generation
          "MCP_TOOL" - MCP protocol tool call
    name: Optional span name (defaults to function name)
    description: Human-readable description
    version: Version identifier for tracking changes
    tags: List of tags for filtering/grouping
    capture_input: Whether to capture function input (default: True)
    capture_output: Whether to capture function output (default: True)

    # Agent-specific parameters (when kind="AGENT"):
    role: Agent role description (also sets agent.name)
    goal: Agent goal/objective

    # Tool-specific parameters (when kind="TOOL" or kind="MCP_TOOL"):
    tool_name: Tool identifier
    parameters: Tool parameter schema

    # End-user identity (typically only on the WORKFLOW root):
    end_user_id: Identifier of the END-USER this trace belongs to — the user
          of your application, not the operator running the SDK. One end-user
          per trace; the backend rolls it up to the trace + session for
          filtering/analytics. Distinct from init(user_id=...).
    end_user_metadata: Optional dict of arbitrary end-user fields, stored as
          JSON on the trace (e.g. {"plan": "pro"}).

    Note: MCP_TOOL automatically handles:

Returns:
    Decorated function with span instrumentation

Examples:
    Top-level workflow:

    >>> @span(kind="WORKFLOW", name="support_workflow")
    >>> def handle_support(query: str):
    ...     docs = retrieve_docs(query)
    ...     return generate_answer(docs)

    Agent with role:

    >>> @span(kind="AGENT", role="Researcher", goal="Find relevant papers")
    >>> def research_agent(topic: str):
    ...     return search_and_analyze(topic)

    Generic processing step:

    >>> @span(kind="CHAIN", name="data_preprocessing")
    >>> def preprocess(data):
    ...     cleaned = clean(data)
    ...     return validate(cleaned)

    Tool/function call:

    >>> @span(kind="TOOL", tool_name="web_search")
    >>> def search_web(query: str):
    ...     return requests.get(f"https://api.search.com?q={query}")

    Retrieval operation:

    >>> @span(kind="RETRIEVER", name="vector_search")
    >>> def retrieve_docs(query: str):
    ...     return vector_db.search(query)

    MCP tool with auto Pydantic handling:

    >>> @span(kind="MCP_TOOL", tool_name="add_numbers", description="Add two numbers")
    >>> async def add(a: int, b: int) -> str:
    ...     return f"Result: {a + b}"

Note:
    This decorator is for instrumenting YOUR custom code. Framework code
    (LangChain, LlamaIndex, OpenAI, etc) is auto-instrumented and doesn't
    need decoration.

1: # NeatLogs CLI
2: 
3: Use the CLI to inspect and manage your NeatLogs projects from a terminal or an automation agent.
4: 
5: The CLI and public API currently support the approved NeatLogs cloud deployments
6: and explicitly enabled localhost development only. Self-hosted deployments are
7: not supported; existing credentials do not bypass this restriction. Self-hosted
8: dashboard, SDK ingest and legacy Swirls integration use are unaffected. See the
9: [deployment policy](../backend/docs/public-api/v1.md#supported-deployments).
10: 
11: ## Choose the right credential
12: 
13: ```mermaid
14: flowchart LR
15:   Start{"Who is using the CLI?"}
16:   Human["Human"]
17:   Agent["AI agent or CI"]
18:   App["Application sending traces"]
19:   OAuth["Browser login or Device Flow"]
20:   ServiceToken["Service-account token"]
21:   IngestKey["Ingest credential"]
22:   Vault["Stored in the OS credential vault"]
23:   SecretStore["Provided by an agent or CI secret store"]
24:   AppSecret["Provided to the SDK as an application secret"]
25: 
26:   Start --> Human --> OAuth --> Vault
27:   Start --> Agent --> ServiceToken --> SecretStore
28:   Start --> App --> IngestKey --> AppSecret
29: ```
30: 
31: - Humans use browser OAuth or Device Flow.
32: - Codex, Claude Code, CI, and other unattended clients use a service-account token.
33: - SDKs and applications use an ingest credential to send traces.
34: 
35: ## Human quickstart
36: 
37: The stable release candidate in this checkout is `neatlogs-cli@0.1.0`, under
38: the MIT license in [LICENSE](LICENSE). It is not published by a source change.
39: Verify `npm view neatlogs-cli@0.1.0 version` before using the stable install
40: command; the currently published team-test release remains available through
41: `npm install --global neatlogs-cli@team-test` until the reviewed release ships.
42: 
43: 1. Install the CLI and confirm that it runs.
44: 
45:    ```bash
46:    npm install --global neatlogs-cli@0.1.0
47:    neatlogs --version
48:    ```
49: 
50:    The stable candidate is `0.1.0`; publication must be independently verified.
51:    Use Node.js 22 or
52:    24. The complete dev setup and verification flow is in the
53:    [team quickstart](../backend/docs/public-api/dev-team-quickstart.md).
54: 
55: 2. Save the host, select the profile, and sign in.
56: 
57:    ```bash
58:    neatlogs profile set work --host '<https-app-origin>'
59:    neatlogs profile use work
60:    neatlogs auth login
61:    ```
62: 
63:    An interactive terminal opens browser OAuth and prints the URL as a
64:    copy/paste fallback. A non-interactive or headless terminal automatically
65:    uses Device Flow; `--device` selects it explicitly.
66: 
67: 3. List the projects you can access.
68: 
69:    ```bash
70:    neatlogs projects list
71:    ```
72: 
73: 4. Save the project you want this profile to use.
74: 
75:    ```bash
76:    neatlogs profile set work --host '<https-app-origin>' --project '<project-uuid>'
77:    ```
78: 
79: 5. Check your identity and read recent traces.
80: 
81:    ```bash
82:    neatlogs whoami
83:    neatlogs traces list --limit 10
84:    ```
85: 
86: `profile set` stores non-secret host and project preferences. Login stores the
87: OAuth credentials separately in the native operating-system vault.
88: 
89: ## US and EU profiles
90: 
91: One CLI package supports both regions. Use the dashboard origin, not the SDK
92: ingest/backend URL, as the CLI host:
93: 
94: ```bash
95: neatlogs profile set us --host '<us-dashboard-origin>'
96: neatlogs profile set eu --host 'https://eu.app.neatlogs.com'
97: neatlogs --profile eu auth login
98: neatlogs --profile eu projects list
99: neatlogs profile set eu --host 'https://eu.app.neatlogs.com' --project '<eu-project-uuid>'
100: neatlogs --profile eu traces list --limit 10
101: ```
102: 
103: The EU backend uses `https://eu.ingest.neatlogs.com`, but OAuth discovery and
104: public API requests stay on `https://eu.app.neatlogs.com`. Sign in separately
105: for each profile; US credentials do not authorize EU requests. Region support
106: requires the frontend, backend, schema and runtime configuration to be deployed
107: there first. See the [EU release preflight](../backend/docs/public-api/eu-release.md).
108: 
109: ## Completion and bounded pagination
110: 
111: Generate completion from the installed CLI command tree, then regenerate it
112: after each CLI upgrade:
113: 
114: ```bash
115: # bash
116: source <(neatlogs completion bash)
117: 
118: # zsh
119: source <(neatlogs completion zsh)
120: 
121: # fish
122: neatlogs completion fish | source
123: ```
124: 
125: Cursor-list commands support bounded multi-page collection. Both flags are
126: required together, and the ceiling is 1 through 1,000 items:
127: 
128: ```bash
129: neatlogs traces list --all --max-items 500
130: ```
131: 
132: When the ceiling truncates the result, the response retains the next cursor so
133: the caller can resume.
134: 
135: ## Request only the permissions you need
136: 
137: ```bash
138: # Default read-oriented login
139: neatlogs --profile work auth login
140: 
141: # Add only the write permissions required for evaluation work
142: neatlogs --profile work auth login \
143:   --scope context:read observability:read evaluation:read evaluation:write offline_access
144: ```
145: 
146: The consent page lists only the permissions requested by this login command.
147: `offline_access` allows refresh tokens; it is not an API permission shown by
148: `whoami`.
149: 
150: ## Agent and CI automation
151: 
152: In **Settings → Service Accounts**, create a dedicated account, bind only the
153: required projects and role, and choose the minimum scopes. Inject
154: `NEATLOGS_TOKEN` through the agent or CI secret store; environment tokens are
155: never written to the OAuth keychain.
156: 
157: ```bash
158: export NEATLOGS_TOKEN='<service-account-token>'
159: export NEATLOGS_PROJECT_ID='<project-uuid>'
160: export NEATLOGS_HOST='<https-api-origin>'
161: 
162: neatlogs projects current --json
163: neatlogs whoami --json
164: neatlogs traces list --limit 10 --json
165: ```
166: 
167: Revoking the access token immediately stops later requests without disabling
168: the service account. `NEATLOGS_API_KEY` remains a legacy fallback; if it and
169: `NEATLOGS_TOKEN` are both set, they must contain the same value.
170: 
171: ## Credential storage and security
172: 
173: Human login uses Authorization Code with PKCE and an exact `127.0.0.1`
174: callback when stdin is interactive. It prints the authorization URL before
175: waiting so it can be opened manually if the browser launch fails. A
176: non-interactive terminal automatically selects Device Flow, and `--device`
177: selects Device Flow explicitly. OAuth access and refresh tokens are bound to
178: the exact host, issuer, and profile, then stored in macOS Keychain, Windows
179: Credential Manager, or Linux Secret Service.
180: 
181: The CLI does not consult Git credential configuration and never silently falls
182: back to a file. Linux requires libsecret and a running Secret Service
183: implementation; the CLI does not fall back to the kernel keyring or a file when
184: that service is unavailable. On POSIX, protected plaintext storage is available
185: only with `--allow-file-credentials`; it uses directory mode `0700`, file mode
186: `0600`, and warns whenever it is used. Windows rejects that option because
187: equivalent ACL enforcement is not implemented.
188: 
189: Credentials are never accepted as command-line flags. The CLI never follows
190: redirects, executes arbitrary API URLs, or fetches a live API schema. Recognized
191: `nloa_`, `nlsa_`, and `nlpk_` prefixes select exactly one credential class; a
192: foreign or mismatched prefix is rejected without fallback.
193: 
194: `schema` inspects the release-embedded contract, not active deployment flags.
195: Each operation carries `x-neatlogs-operation-gate`; only `always` is enabled by
196: default, while every other gate must be enabled by the server before the
197: operation is callable.
198:

341: 
342: For confidential or multiline prompt text, prefer bounded stdin so content is
343: not exposed in shell history or process arguments. Prompt content is limited to
344: 60 KiB within the Public API's 64 KiB JSON request ceiling:
345: 
346: ```bash
347: neatlogs prompts create --name support-answer --content-stdin < prompt.txt
348: neatlogs prompts create --body-stdin < complete-prompt-request.json
349: ```
350: 
351: Use `--body-stdin` when messages, variables, configuration, or commit metadata
352: are also sensitive. It is mutually exclusive with individual prompt field
353: options and validates the complete request before sending it.
354: 
355: Version creation and label activation are intentionally separate authorization
356: steps: `prompts create` requires prompt write access, while `prompts label`
357: requires prompt management access.
358: 
359: `api` accepts only operation IDs with an explicit handler compiled into this
360: CLI release. `--param` and `--query` accept bounded `name=value` pairs, reject
361: duplicates, and are checked against that operation's embedded parameter
362: allowlist before any request. Body-bearing safe reads accept one object from
363: `--body-stdin`, bounded to 64 KiB and validated against the embedded request
364: schema before any request. `schema` commands are offline and do not require credentials.
365: `schema list` and `schema search` return concise descriptors. `schema show`
366: returns the normalized embedded operation contract, including request and
367: response schemas, authentication requirements, and execution/risk metadata.
368: New schema operations default to non-executable until an explicit handler and
369: risk classification are added.
370: 
371: Raw `api` execution fails closed for operations that require target-specific
372: destructive confirmation. Use the operation's curated command instead; raw
373: execution intentionally has no generic `--confirm` flag because confirmation
374: bindings differ by resource.
375: 
376: Feedback and webhook bodies use bounded stdin so comments, expected responses,
377: destination URLs, and write-only webhook secrets do not appear in process
378: arguments. Integration status is local and redacted; it does not discover
379: providers, decrypt credentials, or contact external services.
380: 
381: Organization discovery is OAuth-only. Organization list requires
382: `context:read` plus current `org:read`; detail requires `organization:read`
383: plus current `org:read`. Project discovery accepts OAuth or service-account
384: tokens, requires `context:read` plus current `project:read`, and sends no
385: `x-project-id`. Legacy credentials and an explicitly selected project are
386: rejected locally for all discovery commands.
387: 
388: Account profile and notification-preference reads are OAuth-only and require
389: `profile:read`. Profile ignores a globally configured project and never sends
390: `x-project-id`; it exposes `avatarConfigured`, never an avatar URL. Notification
391: preferences require `--project` or `NEATLOGS_PROJECT_ID`, bind the current user
392: to that selected project, and print all channel, digest, Slack-DM, and
393: quiet-hours settings. Service-account and legacy credentials are rejected
394: locally before a request.
